prompt: Can a carry out occur without signed overflow?
answer: Yes. In four bits, 1111+0001 yields 0000 with carry 1. Signed −1+1=0 fits. Carry checks the unsigned range; signed overflow checks the two’s-complement range.
reason: Separate two independent interpretations of the same bit addition.

prompt: Why does two’s complement represent one more negative value than positive?
answer: Zero uses one of the nonnegative patterns. The n-bit range is −2^(n −1) through 2^(n −1)−1. For six bits it is −32 through 31, not −31 through 31.
reason: Blocks the incorrect lower bound found in CO Notes.

prompt: What must be preserved when widening a signed two’s-complement value?
answer: Its integer value. Repeat the sign bit: five-bit 10110 (−10) becomes eight-bit 11110110. Zero-extending it to 00010110 would represent+22.
reason: Shows why copying bits with the wrong extension changes meaning.

prompt: How do LEA and a memory-source MOV differ at the same displacement?
answer: LEA returns base+displacement. MOV reads the stored value at that address. Compute the address first, then decide whether the instruction dereferences it. Neither address calculation alone nor LEA reveals uninitialized memory.
reason: Targets the address-versus-value distinction without extending the simulator.

prompt: Do cache ways consume additional set-index bits?
answer: No. The index selects a set; all ways in that set are candidates for tag comparison. With capacity C bytes, block size B and W ways: sets=C/(B×W), offset bits=log₂B, index bits=log₂sets.
reason: Distinguishes number of sets from total cache lines.

prompt: Why can a pipeline complete one instruction per cycle without one-cycle instruction latency?
answer: Different instructions occupy different stages. In an ideal k-stage, one-cycle-per-stage pipeline, each instruction still takes k cycles. N instructions take k+N−1 cycles from first start to final completion, before extra stalls.
reason: Separates latency, steady-state throughput and fill/drain cost.

prompt: If q is necessary for p, may q be true while p is false?
answer: Yes. The requirement is p→q: p cannot be true without q. It does not require q→p. The valuation p=false, q=true satisfies the original requirement.
reason: Blocks the reversed parenthetical claim in R&L Notes.

prompt: What changes when forming a contrapositive rather than a converse?
answer: For p→q, reverse the direction AND negate both parts to get ¬q→¬p. Reversing alone gives the converse q→p, which need not be equivalent. Verify equivalence over all valuations.
reason: Uses operation-level recall rather than memorizing one story.

prompt: Does “not everyone has P” require that nobody has P?
answer: No. ¬∀x P(x) means ∃x ¬P(x): one counterexample suffices. “Nobody has P” is ∀x ¬P(x), a different claim. Keep the quantifier’s scope explicit.
reason: Separates one counterexample from failure at every object.

prompt: Can an open formula P(x) be evaluated without adding a quantifier?
answer: Yes, when a structure and an assignment for free x are supplied. A quantifier binds x and ranges over the domain; an assignment chooses its current object. Constants get their meanings from the structure.
reason: Corrects the summary’s overstatement that unquantified variables have no meaning.

prompt: For a contradiction proof of P→Q, which assumptions do you keep and add?
answer: Keep the hypotheses, including P, and temporarily assume ¬Q. Derive a contradiction from these together and justify every step. Do not negate a known hypothesis instead of the target.
reason: Blocks a misleading proof-method note without scoring proof text.
